A 36-year-old patient, primigravida, was admitted to the 
 Department of Gynaecology and Obstetrics 1 month before term 
because of low back pain, painful muscle spasms and rigidity 
of femoral musculature bilaterally preventing normal walking.
Her personal history revealed she had suffered sensorimotor poly-
radiculoneuritis (Guillain-Barré) 18 years before, while family 
history showed no data on autoimmune or hereditary diseases.

On admission, the patient was conscious, with normal cranial 
nerve function. The signs of meningeal syndrome were negative. 
Reduced foot dorsiflexion and absence of triceps surae reflex were 
observed bilaterally as polyradiculoneuritis sequelae. Other myo-
static and abdominal skin reflexes were normal. There were no 
signs of hemi- or paraparesis. Elevated tone of the quadriceps 
muscle of the thigh and painful passive thigh movements were 
present bilaterally. She had walking difficulties due to stiffness 
and painful spasms in the proximal musculature of both lower 
extremities. She also moved slowly because rapid movements in-
duced severe spasms, while heel-toe gait was impossible. Lasègue’s 
and Babinski’s signs were negative; sense of touch, coordination 
and sphincter function were normal, and so was her somatic sta-
tus. She suffered from depression.
  Complete haematology, biochemistry, coagulation and immu-
nological blood tests were normal. Serological testing for syphilis, 
hepatitis and human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) were nega-
tive. The serum GAD IgG titre was elevated (28.7 IU/ml; normal

bryonic antigen (CEA), CA-19.9, CA-15.3 and CA-125 were nega-
tive. Blood levels of thyroid hormones and glycosylated haemo-

1c ) were normal.
  Cerebrospinal fluid examination: cell count 7/3 white blood 
cells; protein 0.475 g/l (normal range 0.10–0.30); normal glucose, 
lactate and chloride levels; oligoclonal bands were negative. Se-
rum amphiphysin and gephyrin antibody titres and cerebrospi-
nal fluid anti-GAD were not determined.
  Electroencephalography, fundus oculi, thyroid, breast, ab-
dominal and pelvic ultrasonography and colour Doppler ultra-
sonography of lower extremity vessels were normal. Electromy-
ography showed continuous motor unit activity with normal 
morphology that was especially pronounced in lumbar paraspi-
nal muscles and femoral muscles bilaterally. Myotonic poten-
tials were absent. The activity resolved with benzodiazepines (10 
mg diazepam i.v. ultrasonography over 1–2 min) ( fig. 1 ). Simul-
taneous continuous motor activity was noted in opposing mus-
cles. Electroneurography showed normal motor and sensory 
conductivity velocities for both common peroneal nerve and su-
ral nerve, with normal compound muscle action potentials and 
sensory nerve action potentials amplitudes. F-wave latencies for 
common peroneal nerve and tibial nerve were normal bilater-
ally.
  The diagnosis of anti-GAD-positive SPS was made based on 
the clinical, laboratory and electromyoneurography criteria ac-
cording to Gordon et al.  
[2]  and Lorish et al.  [3] . Therapy with low 
doses of diazepam (5 mg per os t.i.d.) was initiated, resulting in 
improvement of the clinical picture, alleviation of pain in the 
lumbar region and reduction of rigidity and spasms of femoral 
musculature, which in turn led to walking improvement. The pa-
tient gave birth to a healthy baby born at term by caesarean sec-
tion under general anaesthesia. After delivery, the patient re-
ceived bromocriptine for lactation suppression; also, baclofen
(5 mg per os t.i.d.) was added to the therapy. Then, additional 
work-up was performed including lung x-ray, x-ray of the pelvis 
and both coxofemoral articulations, mammography, and multi-

slice computed tomography of the brain, thorax, abdomen and 
lumbosacral spine, all producing normal findings. Complete re-
mission was achieved in 2 weeks of the delivery. The anti-GAD65 
titre in the infant’s serum was negative.
  Discussion 
 To our knowledge, this is the first report of a patient 
with autoimmune GAD65-positive SPS diagnosed in 
pregnancy. GAD is an enzyme necessary for the synthe-
sis of  /H9253 -aminobutyric acid (GABA), an inhibitory neu-
rotransmitter. GABA deficiency leads to a disbalance of 
excitatory and inhibitory effects on  /H9251 -motoneurons local-
ized in anterior horns of the spinal cord, and consequen-
tially to stiffness of the musculature and involuntary 
muscle spasms. The autoimmune form of SPS can be com-
pared with the less infrequent autoimmune neurological 
disorders such as multiple sclerosis and myasthenia gra-
vis. It is common to all these entities that pregnancy can 
lead to their exacerbation or remission. Relapses mostly 
occur at the beginning of pregnancy, shortly before or af-
ter delivery, whereas remission persists for most of the 
gestational period because of physiological immunosup-
pression.

As our pa-
tient was administered low doses of symptomatic therapy 
(diazepam and baclofen), she probably had spontaneous 
postpartum remission.

Great caution is warranted
in anaesthesia for possible postoperative hypotonia due
to cumulative GABA-ergic action of anaesthetics and
GABA-mimetics generally used by SPS patients. Reaching 
the accurate diagnosis of the syndrome may frequently be 
a long-term process to rule out the paraneoplastic variant 
of the syndrome (found in carcinoma of the breast, lung, 
colon and kidney, thymoma and Hodgkin’s lymphoma).

In conclusion, pregnancy as a physiological event rep-
resents a test for the woman’s health status. As there are 
no uniform guidelines on the management of pregnant 
women with SPS, a multidisciplinary approach with close 
cooperation of the neurologist, gynaecologist-obstetri-
cian, anaesthesiologist and paediatrician-neonatologist 
is warranted in the disease control and pregnancy/deliv-
ery monitoring. In pregnant women with SPS, the intro-
duction of any therapeutic procedure should be preceded 
by weighing the possible therapeutic effect against the 
potential damage to the foetus. Considering the clinical 
picture of SPS patients, caesarean section is the method 
of choice for pregnancy termination.
